sections.title: Cloud Infrastructure
sections.content:
CLOUD DEPLOYMENT MODELS
Model | Description
Public (multi-tenant) | Offered over the Internet by a CSP; subscription or pay-as-you-go; shared-resource performance/security risk
Hosted Private | Third-party hosted, exclusive to one org; more secure/performant, more expensive
Private | Fully owned/operated by the org; on-site or off-site; greatest control (banking, government)
Community | Several orgs share a hosted-private or private cloud to pool costs/policy (e.g. shared standardization)
Hybrid | Combination of the above, e.g. private cloud most of the year, bursting to public cloud at peak demand
Multi-cloud = using multiple CSPs (not the same as hybrid, which mixes ownership models).
SECURITY CONSIDERATIONS BY ARCHITECTURE
Architecture | Security Profile
Single-tenant | Dedicated infrastructure — highest security, customer manages/secures it, most expensive
Multi-tenant | Shared infrastructure, logically separated data — cost-effective, higher risk of leakage/unauthorized access if misconfigured
Hybrid | Sensitive data on private, less-sensitive workloads on public — flexible but needs careful integration/security management
Serverless | Provider manages/secures infrastructure and auto-scales — customer still must secure app access/data
HYBRID CLOUD CHALLENGES
• Managing multiple environments + enforcing consistent policy across them
• Confusion over the on-premises/public-cloud boundary → unauthorized access
• Multiple providers make uniform policy enforcement harder
• Data replication aids redundancy but risks synchronization/consistency issues
• Legal compliance must hold across both on-prem and cloud components
• SLA enforcement is harder across mixed environments; added latency from large data transfers; monitoring requires specialized tools/expertise
CLOUD SERVICE MODELS (XAAS)
Model | What's Provided | Who Secures the App | Examples
SaaS | Full software application, pay-as-you-go | Provider (customer just uses it) | Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Google Workspace
PaaS | Servers/storage/network + a multi-tier app/database platform | Provider secures the platform; customer secures what they build on it | Oracle Database, Azure SQL Database, Google App Engine
IaaS | Raw servers, load balancers, SAN components | Provider secures physical infra; customer secures nearly everything above it | AWS EC2, Azure VMs, Oracle Cloud, OpenStack
THIRD-PARTY VENDOR MANAGEMENT
• SLA (Service-Level Agreement) — defines uptime/performance/support metrics + penalties/remedies
• Assess vendor security practices: encryption, access controls, vulnerability management, incident response, regulatory compliance
• Vendor lock-in — mitigated via data portability, interoperability, standardization, and multi-cloud/hybrid strategies
SHARED RESPONSIBILITY MODEL
Security is shared, not transferred, between CSP and customer. Split shifts with service model (e.g., OS config is fully CSP-owned under SaaS, shared under IaaS).
Cloud Service Provider | Cloud Service Customer
Physical security of infrastructure | User identity management
Securing compute/storage/network equipment | Data storage geographic location config
Foundational network security (e.g. DDoS protection) | User/service access controls to cloud resources
Cloud storage backup and recovery | Data and application security configuration
Resource isolation among tenants | Protection of OS, when deployed
Tenant identity and access control | Encryption use/configuration, especially key protection
Infrastructure monitoring/incident response |
Managing multi-region datacenters |
CENTRALIZED VS. DECENTRALIZED COMPUTING
Model | Description | Fit
Centralized | All processing/storage at one central server (mainframe, client-server) | Large orgs needing strict control
Decentralized | Processing/storage spread across many locations/devices | Resilience/flexibility over central control
Decentralized examples: blockchain, P2P networks, CDNs, IoT device meshes, distributed databases, TOR.
RESILIENT ARCHITECTURE & REPLICATION
• High Availability (HA) — storage guaranteed ≥99.99% uptime via redundant controllers/pools
• Hot vs. cold storage — hot = faster retrieval, higher cost; cold = slower, cheaper
• Databases need low-latency synchronous replication; backup files tolerate more latency
Regions and Availability Zones — CSPs divide the globe into independent regions, subdivided into availability zones with independent power/cooling/network.
Replication Tier | Scope
Local replication | Within a single datacenter, separate fault/upgrade domains
Regional replication (zone-redundant) | Across multiple datacenters in 1–2 regions
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) | Replicated to a distant secondary region — survives a regional outage
VIRTUALIZATION FUNDAMENTALS
• Hypervisor — software layer that creates and manages virtual machines (VMs), each with virtualized CPU/memory/storage/network
• Type I (bare-metal) — runs directly on hardware (e.g., VMware ESXi, Hyper-V) — used in datacenters/cloud for performance and isolation
• Type II (hosted) — runs as an application atop a host OS (e.g., VMware Workstation, VirtualBox) — used for desktop/test environments
• VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) — hosts full desktop OS instances centrally; users access them remotely
APPLICATION VIRTUALIZATION & CONTAINERIZATION
Type | How It Works
Application Virtualization | A limited form of VDI — client accesses or streams a single hosted app rather than a whole desktop (Citrix XenApp, Microsoft App-V, VMware ThinApp); often paired with clientless HTML5 delivery
Containerization | No hypervisor — OS-level resource separation into isolated "cells," each with allocated CPU/memory but sharing the native kernel; containers can vary distro but not guest OS family (no Windows container on a Linux kernel); best known: Docker
Containerization underpins microservices and serverless architecture and is widely used for mobile corporate workspaces.
SERVERLESS COMPUTING & MICROSERVICES
Serverless — provider manages infrastructure, auto-allocates resources, bills by execution time (not hourly). Apps are built as functions/microservices rather than deployed to VM instances. Examples: AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions.
• Eliminates server patch/admin/file-system management burden
• Heavily event-driven — connection triggers auth, session creation, authorization lookup, app logic, DB read/write, logging
• Network security focus shifts to ensuring the client hasn't been compromised
Microservices — application built as small, modular, independently deployable services, each with one responsibility. Enables independent team scaling/updates but risks integration issues once combined. Often implemented via Infrastructure as Code (IaC) for consistent, automated provisioning.
CLOUD AUTOMATION TECHNOLOGIES
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — manages infrastructure via machine-readable definition files (YAML, JSON, HCL — HashiCorp Configuration Language, used by Terraform/Consul). Version-controlled like any code; ensures consistent, repeatable, low-error deployment across dev/staging/production.
Responsiveness mechanisms:
Mechanism | Function
Load Balancing | Distributes traffic across VMs/containers via proxy intermediaries
Edge Computing | Moves processing closer to data source to cut latency (IoT, CDNs, real-time apps)
Auto-Scaling | Automatically provisions/releases resources to match real-time demand
Software Defined Networking (SDN) — abstracts network functions into three planes:
Plane | Role
Control | Decides prioritization, security, switching of traffic
Data | Executes switching/routing and access control
Management | Monitors traffic conditions and network status
SDN application defines policy on the control plane → northbound API to the SDN controller → southbound API to network devices. NFV (Network Functions Virtualization) — rapid deployment of virtual networking via general-purpose VMs/containers.
CLOUD ARCHITECTURE CONSIDERATIONS
Factor | Notes
Cost | Shift from CapEx (up-front hardware/license/setup) to OpEx (pay-as-you-go); unoptimized workloads can erode savings
Scalability | Scale-up (vertical — more CPU/RAM/storage on existing resource) vs. scale-out (horizontal — more instances in parallel)
Resilience | Redundant hardware, clustering, cross-datacenter replication
Ease of Deployment | Automation, standardized templates/images, portability (avoids lock-in)
Ease of Recovery | Automated backup/restore, multi-datacenter failover, geographic disaster recovery replication
SLA / ISA | SLA = performance/availability/support commitments. ISA (Interconnection Security Agreement) = security requirements/responsibilities (encryption, access control, vulnerability mgmt, data segregation, ownership, audit rights, subcontractor handling); must map to regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS)
Power | Efficient hardware/cooling, redundant power (multiple feeds, generators, UPS); PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) — lower is more efficient
Compute | Elasticity, resource pooling, orchestration, automation, serverless — combine for scalable cost-effective compute
CLOUD SECURITY CONSIDERATIONS
• Data protection — data lives outside org-managed infrastructure; misconfiguration risk is high; access controls + encryption + disaster recovery planning are essential
• Patching — depends on CSP's patch policy/response speed; complexity and lack of customer control over underlying infrastructure can make timeline/regulatory compliance difficult
SECURE COMMUNICATION AND ACCESS
Technology | Function
SD-WAN (Software-Defined WAN) | Connects branch offices/datacenters/cloud over a WAN; encrypts traffic, prioritizes/segments by application, integrates with firewalls, centralizes policy management
SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) | Combines WAN tech + cloud-delivered security under a zero trust model; incorporates IAM (assume untrusted until authenticated/authorized); provides IPS, malware protection, content filtering

sections.title: Embedded Systems and Zero Trust Architecture
sections.content:
EMBEDDED SYSTEMS
Purpose-built computing embedded in a larger device: home appliances, smartphones/tablets, automotive (engine control, airbags), industrial automation (robots, sensors), medical devices (pacemakers, insulin pumps), aerospace/defense (navigation, control).
REAL-TIME OPERATING SYSTEMS (RTOS)
Purpose-specific OS designed for stability + processing speed in time-critical applications.
Example | Domain
VxWorks | Aerospace/defense — aircraft control, missile guidance
FreeRTOS | Open-source — robotics, industrial automation, consumer electronics
AUTOSAR | Automotive standard framework using RTOS for engine/transmission/safety systems
Siemens SIMATIC WinCC | Industrial process control/factory automation
Risks — complex, hard-to-secure code; a system-level breach can disrupt critical processes and cause physical harm (medical devices, ICS).
INDUSTRIAL CONTROL SYSTEMS (ICS)
Term | Meaning
ICS | Systems that control machinery in critical infrastructure (power, water, health, telecom, national security)
DCS (Distributed Control System) | ICS managing process automation within a single site
PLC | Embedded controller linked via OT fieldbus/industrial Ethernet to actuators (valves, motors, breakers) and sensors
HMI (Human-Machine Interface) | Local panel or software for PLC output/configuration
Data Historian | Database logging all control-loop data
SCADA | Supervisory system replacing a control server across large, multi-site ICS; uses WAN links (cellular/satellite) to reach field devices
ICS/SCADA sectors: energy/utilities, industrial (mining/refining), fabrication/manufacturing, logistics, facilities (HVAC/lighting/security).
Historically built without IT security in mind. Stuxnet — famous worm that attacked SCADA software controlling Iranian nuclear centrifuges. NIST SP 800-82 covers ICS/SCADA security recommendations.
Industrial systems prioritize safety first, then reverse the CIA triad to AIC (Availability, Integrity over Confidentiality) because hazardous electromechanical processes must keep running safely.
INTERNET OF THINGS (IOT)
Network of physical devices/sensors/actuators exchanging data, usually via cloud back-ends for analytics.
Component | Role
Sensor | Detects environmental changes (temp, humidity, motion)
Actuator | Performs an action based on sensor data (turns on a light, adjusts thermostat)
Examples: smart homes, smart cities (traffic, air quality), healthcare wearables/implants, agriculture (soil/weather/crop monitoring).
Adoption drivers: falling sensor costs, better connectivity (5G, low-power wireless), an explosion of data enabling ML/AI analytics, and (per the text) pandemic-driven remote monitoring/telemedicine growth.
Security risks:
• Limited processing/memory power → weak built-in security controls
• Lack of standardization → integration and mismatched security requirements across devices
• High data volume → harder to secure, bigger breach surface
• Design bias toward functionality/low cost over security; rushed to market without security testing
• Low user/organizational awareness (default passwords unchanged, firmware not updated)
Notable incidents: Mirai botnet (mass IoT-device DDoS), casino hacked via a smart fish-tank thermometer, compromised baby monitors/home security cameras.
Best practice frameworks: IoT Security Foundation (IoTSF), Industrial Internet Consortium (IIC) Security Framework, Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) IoT Security Controls Framework, ETSI IoT Security Standards.
DEPERIMETERIZATION AND ZERO TRUST
Deperimeterization — shifts security focus from network boundaries to protecting individual resources/data directly (robust authentication, encryption, access control, continuous monitoring), because cloud + remote work + mobile have eroded the traditional "inside vs. outside" boundary.
Drivers: cloud (spread infrastructure), remote work (expanded footprint, insecure home networks), mobile devices (unpatched, lost/stolen), outsourcing/contracting (external network as an entry point), unsecured/well-known Wi-Fi keys.
NIST SP 800-207 defines Zero Trust as moving defenses from static network perimeters to focus on users, assets, and resources — "never trust, always verify."
Zero Trust benefits:
Benefit | Description
Greater security | All users/devices/apps authenticated + verified before access
Better access controls | Stringent limits on who/what/where
Improved governance/compliance | Limited data access, better activity visibility
Increased granularity | Access to only what's needed, when needed
Essential ZTA components: network/endpoint security, IAM, policy-based enforcement, cloud security, network visibility, network segmentation, data protection, threat detection/prevention.
Core Zero Trust concepts:
Concept | Meaning
Adaptive identity | Identity verification is continuous, based on current context, not a one-time event
Threat scope reduction | Need-to-know access only — shrinks attack surface and blast radius
Policy-driven access control | Enforced by identity + device posture (security config, patch level, software version) + network context
CONTROL PLANE AND DATA PLANE IN ZERO TRUST
Plane | Component | Role
Control Plane | Policy Decision Point | Defines/updates access policy, monitors for suspicious activity
| — Policy Engine | Evaluates identities, credentials, policies, threat intel, behavioral analytics to make per-request auth decisions
| — Policy Administrator | Issues access tokens, establishes/tears down sessions; sole interface to the data plane
Data Plane | Policy Enforcement Point | Mediates each resource request between subject/system and the resource, communicating with the policy administrator
The session established after approval is an implicit trust zone (e.g., an IPsec tunnel between signed agent, gateway, and resource) — kept as small and transient as possible (ideally per-transaction), unlike perimeter models where trust persists after one login. Even an authenticated session can be terminated if behavioral analytics flags anomalies.
Real-world ZTA examples: Google BeyondCorp, DoD JEDI cloud, Cisco Zero Trust Architecture, Palo Alto Networks Prisma Access.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Assess availability/confidentiality requirements to select the cloud deployment model (public, hosted private, private, community, or hybrid).
• Identify the service provisioning model (software, platform, or infrastructure) that best fits development resources and customization needs.
• Consider advanced concepts where they better fit business needs — microservices, serverless, and orchestration focus on workflow rather than server administration; evaluate SDN benefits/scenarios.
• If using a CSP, create an SLA and security responsibility matrix identifying who performs which security-critical tasks; integrate cloud security reporting/monitoring with on-premises incident response.
• Evaluate the security features of embedded devices and isolate them from other network devices.
• Implement zero trust architecture concepts to validate connections and devices continuously, rather than relying on "inside" and "outside" boundary assumptions.

concept_cards.hook: Centralized platform verifying identity, assigning permissions, and logging actions for an audit trail.
In zero trust architecture, functions defining policy and access decisions.
Classifying cloud ownership/management: public, private, community, hybrid.
Classifying cloud service provision and CSP responsibility limits (SaaS/PaaS/IaaS, etc.).
Cloud deployed for shared use by cooperating tenants.
OS virtualization deployment containing everything to run a service/app/microservice.

practice_questions.q: An attacker modifies the amount on a wire transfer while it is in transit. Which part of the CIA triad was violated?
practice_questions.explanation: Unauthorized modification of data is an integrity failure.

practice_questions.q: In an IaaS cloud model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
practice_questions.explanation: Under the shared responsibility model, IaaS customers manage the OS and above.

practice_questions.q: A sender digitally signs a contract so they cannot later deny having sent it. Which concept does this provide?
practice_questions.explanation: A digital signature ties the message to the signer's private key, preventing denial.

practice_questions.q: A company uses a SaaS email platform. Who is mainly responsible for securing the application code?
practice_questions.explanation: In SaaS the provider manages the application; the customer manages its data and access.

practice_questions.q: In the AAA framework, which step decides what a user is allowed to do after they log in?
practice_questions.explanation: Authorization grants permissions after identity is proven.

practice_questions.q: Defining servers, networks and firewall rules in code files that can be versioned and redeployed is called:
practice_questions.explanation: IaC manages infrastructure through code for consistency.

practice_questions.q: Which element of the AAA framework records what a user did during a session?
practice_questions.explanation: Accounting tracks and logs user activity.

practice_questions.q: Which architecture runs code only when an event triggers it, with the provider managing the servers?
practice_questions.explanation: Serverless functions run on demand without customers managing servers.

practice_questions.q: In a Zero Trust architecture, which component makes the decision to allow or deny an access request?
practice_questions.explanation: The policy engine (part of the control plane) decides; the enforcement point carries the decision out.

practice_questions.q: An application split into many small, independent services that communicate through APIs is called:
practice_questions.explanation: Microservices break an app into independently deployable parts.
